newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Foncier staff to vote on hostage release.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Foncier staff to vote on hostage release.

text.p: Government ministers on Wednesday demanded that staff occupying the Paris headquarters of the troubled French home loans bank Credit Foncier for the sixth day release chairman Jerome Meyssonnier.
"I'm scandalised by this...kidnapping," Justice Minister Jacques Toubon told Europe 1 radio as the bank siege dragged on.

"I want a genuine dialogue to start...so that we can freely discuss the matter and that the holding of the chairman and the board members can be brought to an end," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters.

As the stakes mounted on both sides, trade unions fighting government plans to break up the 145-year-old bank after huge 1995 losses prepared to ballot staff on whether they should release Meyssonnier and under what conditions.

Government-appointed mediator Philippe Rouvillois called on Tuesday for the release of Meyssonnier in a first meeting with the unions, and said in a statement on Wednesday that no further moves in the break-up plan would be taken while talks went on.
The response from several hundred staff in the giant atrium hallway of the Paris headquarters on Wednesday morning was to keep up the fight.
Staff representatives said protesters were ready to dig in their heels if they did not get better guarantees over the fate of around 1,000 jobs.

Meyssonnier and seven of his colleagues have been held since Friday in the protest over the government plans to break up the group, spin off part of it to another cooperatively run lender called Credit Immobilier and wind the rest down over time.

Unions from France's central bank, also fighting cutbacks, joined the fray on Wednesday, highlighting the government's long history of involvement in the banking sector. They demanded that Jean-Claude Trichet, now governor of the independent central bank, be made to account publicly for Credit Foncier's problems.
Trichet was director of the Treasury between 1987 and 1993 when state-owned Credit Lyonnais and Credit Foncier got involved in risky investments which plunged both banks into difficulty.

"He is never questioned about when he was director of the Treasury. There's a kind of reverence which means that certain questions are never asked directly and publicly," Loik Daguzan, member of the CFDT union at the Bank of France, told Reuters.

He said the unions at the central bank and at Credit Foncier had jointly signed a letter to the National Assembly to demand greater public accountability on the grounds that the Treasury was meant to keep tabs on banks, even if Trichet himself was not necessarily directly responsible.

"The only place where he is questioned is in the National Assembly finance commission which, unlike in other countries, is done behind closed doors," he said. Trichet should be made to answer in front of the press, he said.
Arthuis says he has no alternative to the plan for a partial takeover by Credit Immobilier, which would take on 1,500 of the 3,300 staff.

But he is under increasing pressure from intense media coverage of the plight of the bank, founded by Emperor Napoleon III 145 years ago, which has for a long time provided cheap home loans to poorer families with the backing of the state.

Credit Foncier was a stock exchange-quoted company but the government for a long time appointed top management because of its mandate to provide cheap home loans. It has since been taken over, or "nationalised" by the state-owned Caisse de Depots bank as part of the government's wind-up plan.
